To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the FMM is extended to the electrostatic calculations for charges inside a spherical dielectric immersed in an icosolvent by introducing two new fourth-order discrete image approximations of the reaction field, and that these new approximations, together with the FMM, can significantly speed up the calculations of electrostatic interactions in such systems.

the FMM can speed up the electrostatic calculations for charges inside a sphere immersed in an electrolyte solution by a factor of 2.5-5 for 100-1000 point charges, depending on the relative size of the sphere and the Debye length of the electrolyte solution.

the reaction field induced in a dielectric medium by a point charge can be approximated by a set of point image charges with a fourth-order accuracy in terms of the inverse Debye length of the icosahedral multipole expansion, and this approximation can be used to accelerate the calculation of electro-static interactions in a dielectric environment.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the FMM can achieve a 10(2) speedup over direct summation of Coulomb interactions for a large system of charges in a spherical cavity with a dielectric constant of 2, and in an ionic solution with a Debye screening length up to 0.2nm.

the FMM for charges inside a homogeneous dielectric sphere immersed either in vacuum or in an ionic medium has been extended to an accuracy level of 10(-6) with a computational cost of O(N), N being the number of charges.
a 10(-4)-10(-5) relative accuracy for charges inside a 10 Å radius dielectric sphere in a 100 Å radius ionic solvent can be achieved with 3-6 point image charges.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FMM can achieve high accuracy with a very small number of images, which can be used in a wide range of applications.

the FMM can now be used to speedup electrostatic calculations in a variety of applications, ranging from the calculation of the electrostatic interactions of proteins in an aqueous solution to the calculation of the dielectric screening effect on the electrostatic interactions in the protein.

the FMM can provide an efficient alternative for electrostatic calculations in a dielectric medium immersed in an  ionic solvent, and the accuracy can be further improved by including more point image charges.
